content: In the ACTIVE W trial, the combination of aspirin (75-100 mg daily) and clopidogrel (75 mg daily) was found to be statistically less effective than warfarin (target INR 2.0 to 3.0) in managing patients with atrial fibrillation who had one or more risk factors for stroke. The primary endpoint of the study was the first occurrence of stroke, non-central nervous system (CNS) systemic embolism, myocardial infarction, or vascular death. The annual risk of these events was 3.93% in the warfarin group compared to 5.60% in the aspirin/clopidogrel group, resulting in a relative risk of 1.44 (95% CI: 1.18-1.76; p=0.0003). The efficacy of warfarin was less pronounced in patients who were naive to warfarin therapy, although the interaction p-value was not statistically significant. The benefit of warfarin was primarily observed in patients treated at centers where therapeutic INR levels were maintained more than 65% of the time. Importantly, there was no increase in major bleeding events among patients treated with warfarin. In fact, minor bleeding events were more frequent in the aspirin/clopidogrel group (13.6% per year vs. 11.5% per year, p=0.0009). Conversely, patients who experienced bleeding on warfarin would have been excluded from this population.03). The reduction in adverse events with warfarin was primarily attributed to a decrease in stroke and non-CNS embolization. The pathophysiology of stroke in atrial fibrillation is believed to involve embolization of thrombi originating in the left atrium. The findings from ACTIVE W suggest that platelet activation and its inhibition may not play a central role in the prevention of mural thrombus formation and embolization in atrial fibrillation. Warfarin was particularly effective in reducing the incidence of non-disabling strokes rather than disabling strokes. However, there was an observed increase in fatal hemorrhagic strokes, which may explain why warfarin did not demonstrate a reduction in overall mortality in this study. Interestingly, while the combination of clopidogrel and aspirin has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrent myocardial infarction in patients with acute coronary syndromes and presumed plaque rupture, the ACTIVE W trial found a trend toward a higher risk of myocardial infarction in the aspirin/clopidogrel group compared to the warfarin group (0.86% vs. 0.55%, p=0.09). Limitations This trial does not address whether the combination of aspirin and clopidogrel would be non-inferior to warfarin in patients who are naive to warfarin. Notably, 77% of the trial participants were already on warfarin and tolerating it well, while only 23% were warfarin-naive. Among the warfarin-naive patients, no apparent benefit of warfarin therapy was observed.
